title: How far can you jump?
hookLine: a hundred yojanas of water, and a circle of monkeys saying out loud how far each of them can jump
carry: satya: say what you can really do
last: SEVA HEALS THE ONE WHO SERVES.

cards: The job is finally clear, and it's impossible. Sita is in Lanka, an island a hundred yojanas across the ocean. A yojana is an old measure of distance, many miles long.
The monkeys walk down to the shore and look at the water. Valmiki describes it like something alive: huge waves, sea creatures, a roar that never stops. The whole army sits down on the sand, quiet.
Nobody wants to say the obvious thing first.

teach.b: Angada, the young prince who leads them, breaks the silence: who here can cross this? One by one, the monkeys answer honestly. One says he can leap ten yojanas.
Another, twenty. Another, thirty. On it goes, each a little further, up to the old bear Jambavan, who says ninety.
When he was young, he adds, he could have done it easily. He once circled the great god Vishnu when Vishnu strode across the worlds in three steps. But age has taken that.
Then Angada speaks. He thinks he can jump the full hundred.

teach.h: ANGADA: I'M NOT SURE OF THE WAY BACK.
teach.b: What he isn't sure of is the jump back. Jambavan answers kindly but firmly. You're the leader, the root of the whole expedition.
You don't send the root. Nobody brags here, and nobody pretends.
That's a Hindu virtue with a name: satya, truthfulness. In yoga it's one of the yamas, the first restraints a student is asked to keep. And satya isn't only about not lying to others.
It's not lying about yourself: not puffing up your number, and not shrinking it either. Every monkey on that beach tells the truth, the numbers fall short, and that's allowed.
Honest limits are how the right one gets found. This week: a guest fed like a god, a gift that asked nothing, despair on the shore, water for a brother, ego and love, seva, and now satya.
One monkey hasn't spoken. He's sitting apart, saying nothing at all.

how: Readers of the Kishkindha Kanda often linger on this scene of the monkeys stating their limits on the shore, because it sets up the moment when Jambavan turns to Hanuman.

o: an old measure of distance, many miles long
a single leap, the length one monkey can jump
a day's march for an army on foot

p: asks who can cross the sea
told them Sita is in Lanka
an old measure of long distance

s: every monkey claims he can jump the whole sea
each gives an honest, smaller number: ten, twenty, thirty, up to ninety.
Angada thinks he can reach Lanka but isn't sure he can get back
and Jambavan says the leader shouldn't be sent.
Jambavan once circled Vishnu as Vishnu strode the worlds
he remembers it as proof of how strong he used to be.

games.q: you're a monkey on the shore. you can leap thirty yojanas. the prince asks who can cross a hundred. what do you say?
o: a hundred! i'll figure it out in the air.
nothing, so nobody knows my limit.
games.why: each monkey gives his true number: satya, honest about himself, neither puffed up nor hidden.

practice: Bring to mind something that feels too far to cross: a task, a conversation, a long recovery.

Instead of measuring the whole distance, ask honestly how far you can go today, ten yojanas or twenty, and hold that number without shame and without puffing it up. That's satya, turned toward yourself.
With each breath out, let the gap between what you can do and what is needed simply be true, for now.

wordCard.voice: Yojana, an old measure of distance many miles long: what the monkeys count in as each says how far he can jump, and the numbers fall short of a hundred.

orig.note: Sanskrit yojana, an old unit of distance; its exact length varies by source.

carryVoice: Your line: satya, say what you can really do. Not a hundred yet, anyway. Day six hundred two, done.

sources.ref: Valmiki Ramayana, Kishkindha Kanda 64–65 (the monkeys at the shore; how far each can leap)
Yoga Sutras of Patanjali 2.30 (satya among the yamas)
